question: The Electricity Regulation1 establishes criteria for the introduction and operation of capacity markets. Before introducing schemes, countries must conduct and publish national adequacy assessments to identify potential system gaps, and consider a strategic reserve first, as a more cost-effective approach.

If capacity mechanisms are still needed, they must adhere to strict conditions: proportionality and technology neutrality. Despite these requirements, various EU countries are misapplying capacity mechanisms. In Poland, an auction held in July 2025 effectively excluded clean flexibility via a derating factor that strongly favoured gas plants, contradicting the technology neutrality criteria2.

ENTSO-E data showed that the national thermal capacity needs of Greece would not exceed 6 GW3. Yet, the government is planning a capacity market to tender an additional 5.5 GW of liquified natural gas-fired plants. In 2024 the German Government announced a plan to create a capacity market while advancing plans to tender 12.5 GW of gas plants4.

These steps were taken without first publishing a resource adequacy assessment and without respecting technological neutrality. Such examples point to a broader pattern of misuse that could raise consumer energy bills by favouring selected companies, technologies, or national strategies.
Is the Commission aware of this systemic issue, and does it plan to provide clearer legal guidance to ensure capacity mechanisms are applied correctly and prevent further abuses?

Electricity Regulation 2019/943, Articles 20-24. See: https://www.parkiet.com/energetyka/art42157461-blizej-nowych-aukcji-rynku-mocy-dla-elektrownigazowych. Analysis by The Green Tank based on ENTSO-E data: https://thegreentank.gr/en/2024/09/10/thermalcapacity-report/ 12.5GW consisting of 5GW unabated gas plants, 5GW of hydrogen-ready gas plants, 2.5GW hydrogensprinter and batteries.
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (27.3.2026) As the Honourable Member’s request refer to specific ongoing cases, it is the Commission's policy not to comment on concrete cases while they are in progress. Therefore, the Commission’s reply would refer exclusively to the general EU legal framework governing capacity mechanisms (CMs).

The Electricity Regulation1 and the Guidelines on State aid for climate, environmental protection and energy2 set rules for the application of CMs from EU countries, aiming at fostering competition and preventing undue market distortions and limitations to cross-border trade.

CMs should be introduced only when justified by an identified adequacy concern, measured against an economically justified security of supply objective. They must be open to all technologies, new and existing capacity, allow cross-border participation and avoid supporting capacities exceeding the emissions limit from article 22(4) of the Electricity Regulation.
Technical criteria may be set, such as derating factors, to meet the security of supply objective. CMs must also comply with the Union State aid rules.

Annex I of the Clean Industrial Deal State Aid Framework (CISAF)3 recently established a fast-track approval process for CMs meeting requirements based on best practice, including the application of derating factors to account for the real contribution of each type of technology to the adequacy need.
1 Regulation (EU) 2019/943 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 5 June 2019 on the internal market

for electricity (recast), OJ L 158, 14.6.2019, as amended by Regulation (EU) 2024/1747 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 13 June 2024,OJ L, 2024/1747. 2 Communication from the Commission – Guidelines on State aid for climate, environmental protection and energy 2022, C/2022/481, OJ C 80, 18.2.2022, pp. 1–89. 3 Communication from the Commission – Framework for State Aid measures to support the Clean Industrial Deal (Clean Industrial Deal State Aid Framework),C/2025/7600,OJ C, C/2025/3602, 4.7.2025.
